description:
With Valeri Ponzo; the final day of a three-day trip to Walker, Louisiana and back, taking a very circuitous route through the Panhandle to iNat several counties that we had rarely or never visited before. I have now photographed at least one bird species in each of Florida's 67 counties!

As we approached State Road 59 while driving on US-98, at 1530, I had intended to continue driving east so that we would arrive home at a reasonable hour (by 2000). But Val wanted to visit the refuge, saying that she gets to visit maybe once every two years, and since it's 6 miles away and the time was "still early," then we needed to visit. We drove straight to the lighthouse, stopping briefly only at East River Pool/Stony Bayou 1. A strong frontal system moved through east to west at 1650, lasting maybe 25 minutes, and dumping much rain. We were at the lighthouse when the storm hit, so we waited out the worst of it, then drove back north. When we again reached East River Pool/Stony Bayou 1, we were inundated with Eastern Kingbirds heading east or perched in the marsh, in shrubs, and in the few oaks. From 1730 to 1820, we tried to count the size of the flock, which continued moving through for more than 40 minutes and extended for at least one-half mile -- a huge kingbird swarm was visible over the pinewoods to the north. Our estimate of 2,500 Eastern Kingbirds was very likely an underestimate, perhaps by one or more orders of magnitude. Many swallows, including 22 Purple Martins, were also moving east following the storm front. description:
I found this eastern kingbird in the Little Missouri National Grassland a couple of nights ago (5-21-2024), perched in the grass as it waved back and forth in a stiff breeze.  Though it's spring in North Dakota, the somewhat cool nights and days the past week or so have kept the worst of the flying bugs at bay but there are still sufficient numbers to keep the birds busy.  These are among the flycatchers and they often hunt from a perch, flying up to capture a bug, then returning to their perch.  They're also travelers, for they are migratory birds and though they're fairly common in North America, they winter in Central and South America.  

You'll probably see a LOT of "documentary"-style bird images as I experiment with these more often.  Shooting birds-in-flight is akin to shooting skeet the size of pennies, I do believe (and I haven't shot skeet since probably the 90's  lol), with a few unprintable mutters, to boot!  lol
